qa.q: What reason did Mohit have for missing the hostel trek?

grounding: A student notices peers judging the same family-event absence differently and names it gently, including their own part in it.

Outside the kasba college gate, four girls shared a plate of samosas while the bus to the villages idled. Rekha had come in the same faded kurta as Monday, and Deepa murmured, “Second day running, no shame.” The others giggled. Binita arrived late in yesterday's green kurta too, and Deepa beamed. “That green suits you. So simple, so classy.”

Aparna, chewing quietly, counted it in her head. One repeated kurta, two verdicts. When the giggling thinned she said lightly, “Funny, we called it shameless for Rekha and classy for Binita. I think I do that too.”

Deepa opened her mouth and closed it. Binita studied her shoes. Rekha, who had said nothing all along, gave Aparna a tiny nod and pushed the plate toward her.

qa.q: What did Deepa say when she saw Rekha in the faded kurta?
qa.a: Deepa murmured, “Second day running, no shame.”

qa.q: What does Rekha's silence and small nod to Aparna suggest?
qa.a: Rekha felt the whisper stung and was relieved that someone had noticed. The nod and the plate pushed over show quiet thanks.

qa.q: What choice did Aparna make when the giggling thinned?
qa.a: Aparna named the pattern lightly and included herself in it, instead of pointing a finger at Deepa.

qa.q: What might it be like for Rekha to hear Binita praised for the same kurta?
qa.a: It could feel unfair and confusing, as if the cloth mattered less than who wore it, and it might make Rekha doubt herself.

grounding: A student notices others praising one girl and mocking another for the same clothing and names the double standard gently, including themselves.

passage:
In their shared flat in Cape Town, the friends were eating pap and stew when Zanele's phone buzzed for the fifth time. “Sipho again,” she said, smiling.
“So clingy,” said Thandi. “Tell him to get a hobby.” Lerato laughed.
Nadia remembered last week, when Thandi's boyfriend had texted her twenty times during a movie. Everyone had called it sweet.
She waited until the laughter died. Then she said, lightly, “Funny. When Kabelo texts Thandi all night, we say he's romantic. When Sipho does it, he's clingy.”
There was a pause. Thandi opened her mouth, then closed it. “Okay, fair,” she said, and laughed at herself. Zanele looked at Nadia gratefully.

qa.q: How many times had Thandi's boyfriend texted during the movie?
qa.a: He had texted her twenty times.

qa.q: How did Nadia feel as she waited for the laughter to die?
qa.a: She felt uneasy about the unfairness but careful and calm, wanting to point it out without accusing anyone.

qa.q: Why did Nadia's light comment work?
qa.a: She named the double standard with a simple comparison and a light tone, so Thandi could see it and laugh at herself instead of feeling attacked.

qa.q: How might Zanele have felt when Nadia spoke up?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and grateful, since her boyfriend was being judged more harshly for the same thing.

grounding: Shows a student noticing friends judge the same behaviour differently depending on who does it, and naming it gently.

passage:
In the girls' hostel common room, someone played a dance reel by Tina from the other hostel block.
“Attention-seeking,” said Mansi. “Who dances in a corridor?”
“Total drama queen,” agreed Pooja.
Vandana looked at Arohi, curled up on the sofa. Last Sunday Arohi had posted almost the same corridor dance, and the room had cheered, “So talented!”
Vandana didn't want a fight. She said, “Wait, isn't that the same step Arohi did last week? We loved hers.”
Arohi laughed, a little embarrassed. “Oh no. It is.”
Mansi paused. “Hm. Maybe we just like Arohi more,” she admitted. “That's... not really fair to Tina, is it.”

qa.q: Where had Arohi posted her dance?
qa.a: She had posted almost the same corridor dance last Sunday.

qa.q: Why did Vandana choose her words carefully?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable with the unfairness but didn't want a fight, so she asked a gentle question instead of accusing.

qa.q: What did Vandana's question help the group see?
qa.a: It helped them notice they judged the same dance differently depending on who did it, and Mansi admitted it wasn't fair to Tina.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel after the comparison?
qa.a: She seemed a bit embarrassed but good-humoured, laughing as she realised the dances matched.

grounding: Shows a student noticing friends praise one dancer and mock another for the same act, and gently naming the double standard.

passage:
Hey Hemant,
Something's been bugging me since practice, and I'd rather say it to you than to the whole team.
When Rahul skipped two practices last month, we all said he was stressed, poor guy, exams. When Sandeep, the new guy, skipped one this week, we called him lazy and said he doesn't care about the team. I said it too.
I'm not accusing you. I did the exact same thing. I think we go easier on people we already like.
Maybe we could check on Sandeep instead? He might have his own reasons.
Anyway, see you Thursday.
Yogesh

qa.q: How many practices did Rahul skip?
qa.a: Rahul skipped two practices last month.

qa.q: How does Yogesh feel about what the team said?
qa.a: Yogesh feels uneasy and a bit guilty, having said the same unfair thing about Sandeep.

qa.q: What makes Yogesh's message a good way to raise the issue?
qa.a: It's private, includes Yogesh's own part, avoids blame and suggests a kind next step, checking on Sandeep.

qa.q: How might Sandeep be affected if the team keeps judging him this way?
qa.a: He could feel unwelcome and unfairly treated as the new guy, and may pull away from the team.

grounding: A student writes privately to a friend, gently naming how their team judges the same absence differently for insiders and newcomers.

passage:
I'm Swati, and this is about my friends and me, so don't judge too hard.
There are five of us in the flat. Last month Neha from next door skipped the shared cleaning rota twice, and Sarika said, "Typical. She's so entitled." Everyone agreed. Two weeks later Sarika skipped it three times because of her internship, and the verdict was, "Poor thing, she's swamped." I agreed both times. That's the bit that bugged me.
So one night over instant noodles I said, not accusing, just curious, "Funny, when Neha skipped, she was entitled, and when Sarika skipped, she was busy. Maybe Neha was busy too?"
There was a pause. Sarika went a bit red and said, "Okay. Fair." Then Divya said, "I do this with my brother all the time."
Nobody fought. The next week, someone invited Neha over for chai.

qa.q: How many times did Sarika skip the rota?
qa.a: Three times, because of her internship.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling in the days before speaking up?
qa.a: Swati felt uneasy and a bit guilty, having agreed with two opposite verdicts on the same behaviour.

qa.q: Why did Swati's way of raising it work?
qa.a: It was framed as a curious question, "Maybe Neha was busy too?", so nobody felt accused and they could see the pattern themselves.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt when Swati pointed out the pattern?
qa.a: Sarika seemed embarrassed, going a bit red, but not attacked, so she could admit "Okay. Fair."

grounding: Shows a student noticing friends judge the same behaviour differently depending on who does it, and naming it gently so they see it themselves.
